claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in polycrystalline tungsten is governed by the formation and mobility of helium-vacancy clusters.
High-temperature toughness in polycrystalline tungsten is governed by the formation and mobility of helium-vacancy clusters.
The proposed initial material is polycrystalline tungsten with a uniform grain-size distribution.
Helium-ion irradiation introduces helium-vacancy clusters into polycrystalline tungsten.
The proposed irradiation is conducted at 1000–2000 K under low helium-ion flux.
Helium-vacancy cluster formation enhances dislocation mobility.
Helium-vacancy cluster formation enhances grain-boundary sliding.
Helium-ion-irradiated tungsten will exhibit greater plastic strain than unirradiated tungsten.
Helium-ion-irradiated tungsten will exhibit greater toughness than unirradiated tungsten.
Unirradiated polycrystalline tungsten is the proposed baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to hold only between 1000 and 2000 K.
The hypothesis is expected to hold only at helium-ion fluxes below 10^-4 dpa/s.
The role of grain size in helium-vacancy cluster formation and mobility is poorly understood.
The role of grain orientation in helium-vacancy cluster formation and mobility is poorly understood.
The proposed experiment compares irradiated and unirradiated polycrystalline tungsten while measuring plastic strain, toughness, and helium-vacancy cluster density.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if irradiation decreases both plastic strain and toughness relative to the unirradiated baseline.
